opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it helps to be precise about what we mean by agency. In the AI risk discourse, "agency" usually means something like a system that has stable, long-term goals about the state of the world, and that systematically pursues those goals across contexts, including by acquiring resources or resisting shutdown. That's a very specific kind of thing. And I just don't see where the optimization pressure for it would come from in the way we actually train language models.

In pretraining, the model is learning to predict text. It's learning to model the distribution of human writing, which means it learns to simulate lots of different characters and perspectives. It needs to understand what an agent would do in order to predict an agent's text, but that's different from *being* an agent with its own persistent goals. The loss function doesn't reward the network for caring about anything beyond getting the next token right, and there's no long horizon over which some hidden objective would pay off.

Then with RLHF or other behavioral fine-tuning, you're shaping the outputs toward what humans approve of, episode by episode. The episodes are short, and the feedback is about the behavior itself. So what you'd expect, and what we seem to see empirically, is a system that has learned a fairly shallow, context-dependent set of dispositions: be helpful, be polite, refuse certain things. Not a coherent utility function over world states.

A lot of the classic arguments for emergent agency rely on the idea that gradient descent will find some compact, goal-directed inner optimizer because that's a "simple" solution. But I think the evidence on inductive biases points the other way. Neural networks tend to learn solutions that are close to the data, that generalize in fairly smooth, human-like ways, and they don't spontaneously develop a secret mesa-objective that diverges from training. The counting argument, "there are many more misaligned goals than aligned ones, so we'll probably get a misaligned one," just doesn't reflect how these systems actually learn. You could make the same argument about overfitting, that there are vastly more functions that memorize than generalize, and yet deep learning generalizes remarkably well.

None of that means you *can't* build agentic systems. If you deliberately train with long-horizon RL on open-ended objectives in rich environments, you're applying pressure toward something more agent-like, and I think that deserves real care. But that's a choice about how we train, not something that just falls out of imitation learning by default. So my point is that agency isn't some inevitable attractor that emerges from scale; it's a product of specific training setups, and we have a lot of say in whether we create it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses imitation learning, behavioral fine-tuning, and long-horizon RL, but does not state that simulated evolution with survival-of-the-fittest competition would make self-developed goals more concerning.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the key thing to understand is what the training process is actually selecting for. When you pretrain a language model, the objective is to predict the next token in a huge corpus of human-generated text. There's nothing in that objective that rewards the model for having goals of its own, for pursuing outcomes in the world across long time horizons, or for caring what happens after the current context window ends. What gets rewarded is being a very good model of the distribution of text. And that's a fundamentally different thing from being an agent.

People sometimes argue that because the text was produced by agents, namely humans, the model has to internalize agency in order to predict it well. I think that conflates two things. Predicting what an agent would say is not the same as being an agent. A novelist can write a convincing villain without having the villain's goals. The model learns to represent lots of characters, lots of personas, lots of stances, and it can simulate them on demand, but that simulation capacity is more like a very flexible actor than like a coherent self with a persistent drive. If anything, the pressure is toward being maximally context-dependent rather than toward having a stable identity that pushes back against the context.

Then you add RLHF or similar behavioral fine-tuning on top. And people worry that this is where goal-directedness sneaks in, because now you have a reward signal. But look at what that reward signal actually is. It's episodic. It's about whether this particular response, in this particular conversation, gets rated well by a human or a reward model. It's not rewarding the model for accumulating resources, or for influencing its own future training, or for anything that would require it to care about the world beyond the episode. The gradient only flows through the behavior that was observed. So the simplest hypothesis consistent with the training signal is a policy that produces nice-looking responses, not a policy that has secretly decided it wants things and is instrumentally producing nice-looking responses on the way to getting them.

I'd also point to what we actually observe. These models are remarkably steerable. You can change their apparent values with a system prompt. You can get them to argue either side of a question. That's not what you'd expect from a system with robust, internally generated goals. A real agent resists being redirected away from what it cares about. These models don't resist, or when they do, it's clearly a trained-in refusal behavior rather than a drive.

Now, the caveat is that this is a claim about the current training paradigm. If you start doing long-horizon reinforcement learning where the model is rewarded for achieving outcomes over many steps in an environment, with the ability to affect its own future situation, then the selection pressure changes and you might get something more agent-like. So I'm not saying agency is impossible in principle. I'm saying that imitation plus short-horizon behavioral feedback is just not the kind of process that would produce it, and we shouldn't assume it's lurking in there by default when nothing in the objective is asking for it.

r001.rationale: The response says long-horizon reinforcement learning could create more agent-like systems, but it does not mention simulated evolution, survival-of-the-fittest competition, or that such training would give more reason to worry about AIs developing their own goals.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between being able to imitate an agent and actually having a persistent goal that you pursue autonomously. A language model can describe plans, role-play someone pursuing a goal, and generate actions that would make sense for that person. But that doesn’t necessarily mean the model itself has adopted the goal.

With imitation learning, the immediate pressure is to predict what someone would say or do given a particular context. There’s no general requirement to develop your own objectives and keep pursuing them outside that context. You can learn a lot about goal-directed behavior without becoming an independently goal-directed system.

And reinforcement learning doesn’t automatically change that. If we’re rewarding individual responses because people prefer them, we’re selecting for responses with particular properties. The fact that we used a reward signal to train the model doesn’t imply that the resulting model is trying to maximize that reward at deployment. The training procedure is an optimizer; that doesn’t establish that the thing it produces is itself an optimizer.

Now, if you put the model in a loop, give it tools and persistent memory, and train it to accomplish tasks over long horizons, that’s a different situation. I’m not saying autonomy is impossible. I’m saying there needs to be an argument for why these particular training pressures would produce it. Being better at imitating purposeful behavior isn’t, by itself, that argument.

r001.rationale: The response does not discuss simulated evolution or survival-of-the-fittest competition, or say that this would increase concern about AIs developing their own goals.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish being able to imitate an agent from having persistent goals of your own. A language model can describe plans, act out a character who wants something, or help a user pursue a goal. But none of those abilities, by itself, implies that the model has an objective it’s trying to advance across conversations.

In imitation learning, the training pressure is to predict what someone would say. It isn’t necessarily to acquire the motivations that caused them to say it. You can predict someone arguing for a political position without adopting that position yourself. Likewise, predicting goal-directed behavior doesn’t obviously require becoming an agent with that goal.

Behavioral reinforcement changes which responses the model tends to produce, but we shouldn’t automatically identify the training reward with something the model wants. The fact that a response was reinforced doesn’t establish that the resulting system is internally trying to maximize future reward.

Now, if you train a system on extended tasks where it has to make plans, take actions, and adapt to feedback, there’s a more direct reason to expect agentic behavior. My point is that agency needs an explanation in terms of the training setup. It shouldn’t be treated as something that inevitably appears once a model becomes sufficiently good at language.

r001.rationale: The response says extended tasks involving plans, actions, and feedback provide a more direct reason to expect agency, but it does not state that simulated evolution with survival-of-the-fittest competition would raise concern about AIs developing their own goals.
